title: Assurance that stays proportional to each behavioral change

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to keep formally verified software practical to change. Starting with a system whose behavior has already been specified and proved, engineers would implement a requested behavioral change and repair the affected proofs with effort comparable to the software change itself. Repeated functional releases would preserve the applicable guarantees without an increasing proof-maintenance burden. DARPA’s PEARLS program articulated the underlying goal of making proof maintenance comparable in effort to software maintenance.

Concept synthesis: the full proposal combines proportional proof repair with a separate requirement for structural stability. Across a sustained sequence of releases, selected measures of coupling and defects against the specification would not worsen. Proof repair concerns whether the revised implementation still satisfies its revised obligations; structural stability concerns whether continued development makes future changes increasingly entangled. Neither property automatically establishes the other. Here, proportionality means a bounded effort relationship under an explicit accounting rule and a defined workload, rather than a claim that every possible edit has a universally predictable cost.

significance.text: Software maintenance can invalidate formal proofs and require substantial repair work. A reliable way to contain that burden would make strong assurance easier to retain during ordinary development, allowing proofs to participate in the continuing release process. DARPA identifies this integration into normal development, with specialized formal-methods expertise reserved for the hardest cases, as a desired consequence of scalable proof repair.

Conditional impact synthesis: if representative behavioral changes could be implemented and reverified with effort proportional to their size, the direct benefit would be bounded marginal implementation and assurance-maintenance costs within the demonstrated scope. If structural stability were also sustained, a highly assured component could continue receiving features without a measured increase in coupling. This could make long-lived assured products more economically feasible and reduce pressure to choose between maintaining guarantees and shipping changes. These are conditional consequences of the proposed capability, not demonstrated economic outcomes.

Impact limits: proportional proof repair alone would not make total lifecycle cost proportional to behavioral change. Specification work, integration, tooling, deployment and architectural concerns outside the selected metrics could still grow. Nor does a preserved proof establish that the specification captures every user expectation: seL4 explicitly distinguishes its proved properties from expectations that those properties may not cover. A stable coupling measure would likewise provide evidence about that measure, not a guarantee against every form of architectural deterioration.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is dependable, scalable repair of assurance artifacts through sustained functional evolution, with a measured cost relationship to the software work. PEARLS documents limits in the size and complexity of verification problems, the specialized skills required to use verification tools, and the repair effort that maintenance can trigger. PROVERS extends this agenda through tools for proof-friendly system design and reduced proof-repair workload. These sources establish substantial engineering challenges and research objectives; they do not establish that the combined SWE-05 capability is universally unsolved as of November 1, 2026.

Engineering synthesis: candidate barriers include proof dependencies that extend beyond the edited code and implementation relationships that make a local behavioral request require changes across many components. A practical solution would need to identify which obligations remain valid, regenerate or repair those affected, and check the resulting arguments. It would also need to accommodate intentional specification changes: changing the required behavior can require new invariants or contracts, rather than merely repairing a proof script. Non-local dependence and implementation entanglement are plausible mechanisms to investigate, not definitive causal findings established by the retained sources.

Measurement synthesis: the structural and economic parts of the proposal introduce additional barriers. Behavioral-change size needs an operational definition; code churn alone may conceal changes of very different difficulty. Proof costs must include expert intervention, automation and infrastructure upkeep. Structural metrics must be chosen so that apparent stability cannot be obtained merely by moving complexity outside the measured boundary. Even successful automation on many edits would leave the full proposal untested without these longitudinal measurements.

current_state.text: PEARLS provides a historical statement of the maintenance problem and the desired outcome that moderate code changes should lead to moderate automated proof repairs. Its retained program page is marked complete and no longer maintained, and does not report attainment of that full outcome. This omission is not evidence of program failure. The PROVERS page positively reports that PEARLS demonstrated AI and machine-learning support for generating and maintaining software-verification proofs at large scale, while describing further work on proof-friendly design and repair workflows.

The PROVERS FAQ dated May 4, 2023 reports a relevant AWS s2n example: over one year, corresponding proof scripts were corrected automatically after code changes in 953 of 956 cases, with proof engineers needed in the remaining three. This is substantial scoped evidence of proof-maintenance automation. It is DARPA’s account of the example in the supplied review; the underlying experimental data were not independently inspected. The reported counts do not establish the repair-to-code effort ratio, the representativeness of the functional changes, or a stable coupling trend.

The seL4 project reports no functional-correctness defects in verified code since completion of its functional-correctness proof in 2009, a history exceeding fifteen years. Its assurance applies to the verified configurations and the specified properties under the stated assumptions. This provides a strong baseline for the kind of assurance SWE-05 would seek to preserve. It does not establish correctness of unverified configurations or all surrounding system behavior, and the supplied evidence does not quantify seL4’s feature-development velocity, expert proof-maintenance burden or proportional repair costs.

On September 2, 2025, Proofcraft reported that seL4 proofs covered all Arm platforms on which the kernel could run at that time. It highlighted the addition of a 23rd Arm platform that required zero new proof work. This demonstrates valuable reuse and platform generalization within the reported scope. Adding platform support is a different change class from altering specified functionality, so this result does not establish zero-cost repair or proportional maintenance for arbitrary functional releases.

The historical software-aging citation supplied with the research cannot support its earlier detailed attribution here. The retained extraction of the page identified as Parnas’s “Software aging” contains only an IEEE Computer Society site label, with no substantive abstract or paper content. Consequently, the supplied review could not verify the attributed wording, detailed aging account or bibliographic particulars. This is an extraction limitation, not evidence that the paper or its argument is false.

Evidence synthesis: the retained material establishes meaningful progress in automated proof maintenance, long-lived formal assurance and proof reuse. It does not demonstrate the combined capability of sustained functional releases, proportional repair effort and independently stable structure. Because the supplied bounded search record is empty, this is a scoped assessment of the retained evidence rather than a comprehensive account of the field as of November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: begin with a production component whose verified properties, configurations and trusted assumptions are explicitly documented at an assurance level comparable to the relevant seL4 baseline. Pre-register a representative functional-change workload and a release count tied to a named five-year product-line comparator. The comparator should make the intended development horizon concrete; elapsed time or a large number of trivial releases would not alone establish representative functional evolution.
completion_criteria.label: Documented seL4-comparable baseline with pre-registered five-year product-line workload

completion_criteria.text: Proposed effort test: for every release, require proof-repair effort to remain within a preselected small constant factor of code-change effort. Define the units and accounting boundary before the experiment, including expert intervention, automation costs and proof-infrastructure maintenance. Record specification work and implementation work separately, and report exceptional changes rather than hiding them within aggregate averages. The supplied evidence establishes neither a community-standard constant nor a standard release horizon; these thresholds would be explicit experimental choices.
completion_criteria.label: Proof-repair effort within a preselected small factor of code-change effort

completion_criteria.text: Proposed assurance and structure tests: each released verified fragment must satisfy its applicable specification. Invalidated proofs or violations of retained contracts must block release until resolved. Intentional contract changes should create explicit new proof obligations rather than being treated automatically as forbidden changes. A pre-registered coupling metric and trend rule should show no secular growth across the workload. Any claimed absence of specification defects must remain bounded by the verified properties, configurations and assumptions; newly discovered mismatches should be reported and investigated.
completion_criteria.label: Each release satisfies applicable specifications with no secular coupling growth

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundary tests: make the release sequence, specifications, proof artifacts, tool versions, human interventions and cost records available for independent replay where access permits. Replicate the result with independent maintainers and additional components or change classes, documenting failures and scope restrictions. Successful finite trials would establish the breadth and cost behavior demonstrated by those workloads. They would not prove literal universality or an asymptotic proportionality law for all future changes.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replay and finite-trial replication of breadth and cost behavior

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: SWE-01, “Push-button verifying compilation for practical systems,” concerns obtaining implementation assurance through verification and compilation; SWE-02, “Certified synthesis of system-scale programs from reviewable specifications,” concerns generating certified implementations from specifications. Both could supply an initial verified system or tools for regenerating changed portions. SWE-05 focuses on the continuing cost and structural consequences of functional evolution after that baseline exists. Repeated successful verification or synthesis would not by itself establish proportional maintenance effort.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-03, “Demonstrable adequacy of a specification against intent and the environment,” addresses whether the requirements being proved are the right ones. SWE-06, “Sound behavioral recovery of legacy systems,” addresses recovering behavior from existing software. These capabilities could help establish or revise the specifications on which SWE-05 depends. Maintaining a proof through changes neither recovers an unspecified legacy system’s behavior nor establishes specification adequacy.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-04, “A compositional calculus for concurrent systems that fail,” and SWE-10, “Proof-carrying behavioral composition across trust boundaries,” could provide ways to localize reasoning and reuse component guarantees. Such mechanisms may reduce the proof obligations disturbed by a change. Their central concerns are sound composition under concurrency, failure or trust boundaries; SWE-05 additionally asks whether repeated functional changes preserve assurance at a bounded measured cost without worsening selected structural measures.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-07, “Practical confinement of general untrusted programs,” SWE-08, “Sequential meaning for fault-tolerant distributed execution,” and SWE-09, “Observable determinism as the default for parallel systems code,” concern particular guarantees or execution models. Systems providing those capabilities could themselves need proportional assurance maintenance. SWE-05 does not supply confinement, fault-tolerant sequential meaning or observable determinism merely by preserving proofs; those properties must be included in the relevant specifications and demonstrated within their own scopes.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-11, “Proved semantics-preserving transformation of practical systems,” concerns transformations that retain behavior, such as a migration whose semantics are preserved. SWE-05 concerns specified behavioral changes and the updated proofs they require. They may share proof-reuse techniques, but successful behavior-preserving migration does not establish proportional repair through functional evolution. Autonomous runtime repair of production failures and predictive laws of defect rates are also distinct objectives mentioned in the research, although neither has an entry in the supplied roster. No additional historical comparison list was supplied.

The retained seL4 evidence does not quantify functional-release velocity or the human and automated effort required to maintain proofs across such releases.

brief.title: Software that stays provably correct as it changes
possible: People could keep adding features to software backed by mathematical proofs that it meets its stated requirements. Updating those proofs would take effort comparable to changing the code, while repeated releases would avoid making the software’s parts increasingly tangled.
why: For teams maintaining software over many years, this could reduce pressure to choose between shipping features and preserving guarantees. Keeping proof maintenance manageable could make products with strong guarantees more affordable to sustain.

sources.showed: The seL4 project reports no defects that violate specified behavior in its verified code since its correctness proof was completed.
sources.quote:
there have been no functional correctness defects in
  verified code since the functional correctness proof completed in 2009
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates lasting assurance from mathematical proofs checked by software.
sources.not_established: It does not establish how proof-maintenance effort compares with the effort of adding features.

sources.showed: Proofcraft extended seL4 proofs across all supported Arm hardware platforms. An additional platform needed no new proof work.
sources.quote:
Now, the
formal proof covers 100% of the Arm
platforms
that seL4 supports.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates proof reuse when extending hardware support.
sources.not_established: Supporting another hardware platform does not establish comparable proof-repair costs when changing software behavior.

sources.showed: DARPA reports that proof scripts for Amazon’s s2n software were repaired automatically after code changes in all but three cases.
sources.quote:
Workflow integration of this repair technology enabled 
performance enhancements with little involvement of proof engineers.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates extensive automation of proof maintenance in a working software project.
sources.not_established: It does not establish proportional repair effort across representative feature changes or stable relationships between components.

sources.showed: The PEARLS research program sought automated proof repair with maintenance effort comparable to maintaining the software.
sources.cited_for: It states the goal of making proof maintenance part of ordinary software development.
sources.not_established: The program description does not demonstrate that this goal was achieved.

shown: Amazon has demonstrated extensive automatic proof repair. The seL4 project reports lasting correctness guarantees, and Proofcraft has demonstrated proof reuse across hardware platforms. Together, these results establish pieces of the capability.
missing: A sustained sequence of representative feature changes with proof-repair effort bounded relative to code-change effort.
The same releases preserving their guarantees without growing coupling, meaning dependence between software components.
Independent repetitions showing where the combined result holds and where it fails.

milestones.label: A proved starting point and representative workload
milestones.explanation: A production component would need documented guarantees comparable to seL4’s and a workload fixed in advance against a named five-year product line. This would establish a meaningful test of continued development.

milestones.label: Proof repair stays within the agreed effort limit
milestones.explanation: Every release would need proof-repair effort within a small, preset multiple of code-change effort, counting experts and tool upkeep separately from requirements work. This would test whether assurance costs stay proportional.

milestones.label: Every release meets requirements without growing component dependence
milestones.explanation: Each release would need proofs of its applicable requirements, including intentional changes, and no upward trend in a preset measure of component dependence. This would test both correctness and structural stability.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce the results across further cases
milestones.explanation: Independent maintainers would need to replay the releases and repeat the effort and correctness tests on further components or change types. This would establish how broadly the demonstrated result applies.

uncertain: How should the size of a requested behavior change be measured when similar amounts of code can require very different effort?
What effort limit and workload would make a convincing test of sustained development?
Can a measure of component dependence detect deterioration without merely pushing complexity outside its boundary?

page.title: Automated proof repair during software evolution
page.definition: When a change to a program or its specification breaks a proof, a tool adapts the argument and a proof assistant checks that it establishes the required property for the revised program under its stated assumptions. Developers without formal-methods expertise could use this process during routine maintenance.

goal.need: Adding interrupts, ARM page tables and address spaces to the seL4 operating-system kernel took several person-months to design and implement and 1.5–2 person-years to re-verify. Teams can rerun proof scripts with each update, but a broken argument still needs repair. Automating that work would help developers keep guarantees about specified behaviour current as they release changes, with specialist help reserved for difficult cases. Each guarantee depends on the assumptions of its proof.

completion.title: Traditional developers meet the 1% manual-change target for proofs of high complexity software.
completion.criterion: Developers without formal-methods expertise carry out the Phase 3 demonstration on a high-complexity system. Following software update and maintenance, the target is 1% of proof lines requiring manual change.
completion.set_by: DARPA, PROVERS solicitation HR001123S0020, Table 1, Phase 3 column and proof-maintenance row. FAQ A59 specifies who carries out the demonstration.
completion.basis: DARPA labels the table’s targets tentative. Its quantitative evaluation team assesses cost and efficiency separately. The percentage measures manual proof-line edits and supplies no bound on labour or on how changes propagate through the software.

milestones.title: A proof assistant accepts an automatically repaired proof after a program or its specification changes.
milestones.criterion: A change invalidates an existing proof. Automation adapts the proof, and the proof assistant accepts it for the required claim about the revised version under the stated assumptions.
milestones.set_by: Interactive theorem-proving community convention: proof-checker acceptance, described for Coq by Ringer and colleagues in Section 2.
milestones.threshold_quote: Coq compiles it to a low-level representation called a proof term, then checks that the proof term has the expected type.

milestones.title: A development workflow automatically adapts a broken proof and checks it on the software update.
milestones.criterion: Submit an update that invalidates an existing proof. As part of the development workflow, a repair tool adapts the proof and the proof check passes for the updated software and applicable specification. Developers may resolve obligations left by the tool.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, PROVERS solicitation HR001123S0020, TA1.2 Workflow Integration.
milestones.threshold_quote: automatically adapt those proofs in response to changes.

milestones.title: Experts maintain proofs for low complexity software at the 20% manual-change target.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate proof maintenance after a software update on an open, unclassified system of low complexity. Formal-methods experts may participate fully. The Phase 1 target is 20% of proof lines requiring manual change.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, PROVERS solicitation HR001123S0020, Table 1, Phase 1 column and proof-maintenance row. FAQ A59 describes expert participation.

milestones.title: Journeyman developers maintain proofs for moderate complexity software at the 10% manual-change target.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate proof maintenance on a system of moderate complexity with a team that includes programmers without substantial formal-methods backgrounds. Phase 2 includes four specification-change cycles. Its target is 10% of proof lines requiring manual change following software update and maintenance.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, PROVERS solicitation HR001123S0020, Table 1, Phase 2 column and proof-maintenance row. Section I.B describes the team and change cycles.

not_found: No numerical definitions of system complexity or detailed proof-line counting and aggregation rules were found in the PROVERS solicitation or FAQ.
No public evaluation establishing attainment of the PROVERS phase maintenance targets was found in searches of DARPA, the programme portal, performer announcements and papers.
No external completion test combining a proof-repair effort ratio with a longitudinal software-coupling bound was found in PEARLS, PROVERS or proof-maintenance benchmark searches.
No academy, professional society or programme statement disputing the value or feasibility of automated proof repair was found.

finement with super_fix completed the proof.

results.finding: System Capless agents completed 43 of 48 broken-proof repair tasks in Lean 4.
results.detail: The 43 of 48 count covers the full Repair category and cannot be read as a rate specific to specification or invariant changes. For step_masked, a human directed a change to the read and write rules, and the text gives no final check result.
results.quote:
Among proof-related tasks, the agent performs the best for Repair tasks:
90% success rate (43/48), only 8% intervention, and fewer iterations (4.9 checks vs. 8.3 for Proof).

results.finding: In one System Capless mutable-reference update, the agent fixed ten proof issues in Semantics/Props.lean.
results.detail: The agent left sorry placeholders where the original read and write rules allowed access to cells outside the capability set. A human directed the rule correction.
results.quote:
It fixed ten distinct issues,
primarily adding cases for the new operations
and updating proofs to match changed definitions.

results.finding: AWS-LC reported about 16 proof-maintenance fixes across 616 pull requests in 2023.
results.detail: The aggregate count does not identify which pull requests changed implementation logic or how the proofs were repaired.
results.quote: Year 2023, around 16/616(PRs) fixes

results.finding: For one MoveLight vector extension, Claude Code propagated proof changes across 30+ files.
results.detail: The reported workflow used interactive prompts and human guidance. The paper gives no submission record or before-and-after proof-check trace for the vector change.
results.quote:
The vector extension (Sec. 4.1) took
only one day despite changing 30+ files because the modifications were uniform: adding a new
path element vecElem and a new case to the value/type compatibility relation, then threading
them through existing lemmas, so the AI could apply the same pattern repeatedly without errors.

results.finding: CertiGC (n=1 update): 1 Codex-assisted invariant repair passed Rocq checks and merged upstream.
results.detail: Rocq checked the repaired proof. The workflow result itself is documented in a single preprint by the author.
results.quote:
The strongest validation is machine checking. The relevant proof files compile,
and the branch was merged upstream.

results.finding: In one xv6 kernel project, Claude Code agents updated proofs after source changes. The number of repairs was unreported.
results.detail: The reported repairs concern binary changes such as shifted offsets or instruction alignment. The excerpt lists a re-proving evaluation in its contents but ends before presenting its results.
results.quote:
we find that agents are able to perform these tedious proof updates
without substantial developer input.

results.finding: Devoid lifted Coq traversal proofs across data-type changes in 2 tree scenarios, with 0 additional proof obligations for lifting.
results.detail: The multi-step case simulated incremental updates and required intermediate types and unpacking. The reported proof line counts measure generated term size. The source gives no count of manually changed proof lines.
results.quote:
These components were enough forDevoid to lift functions and proofs with
no additional proof burden and no additional axioms.

results.finding: Lean accepted mechanical repairs in 109 of 139 eligible proof failures after structural implementation refactoring.
results.detail: Eligibility was limited to three one-identifier templates for unfold, simp, or dsimp. Lean checked the individual proofs. The aggregate repair count is reported by the preprint authors.
results.quote:
The predefined edit repairs 109/139 eligible failures, including 51/54
reference-proof failures and 58/85 prover failures, with a median edit of two tokens on one line.

case_label = "Change type". Reason: The published classification makes it possible to re-judge results by the kind of change each demonstration actually tested.

definition = "When a change to a program or its specification breaks a proof, a tool adapts the argument and a proof assistant checks that it establishes the required property for the revised program under its stated assumptions. Developers without formal-methods expertise could use this process during routine maintenance.". Reason: The current definition folds a tentative programme target into the meaning of proof repair and leaves the checker’s role implicit.

goal.need = "Adding interrupts, ARM page tables and address spaces to the seL4 operating-system kernel took several person-months to design and implement and 1.5\u20132 person-years to re-verify. Teams can rerun proof scripts with each update, but a broken argument still needs repair. Automating that work would help developers keep guarantees about specified behaviour current as they release changes, with specialist help reserved for difficult cases. Each guarantee depends on the assumptions of its proof.". Reason: The seL4 study measures the cost of verifying a change directly, whereas the existing figures measure the cost of initial verification.
